verdict.reasoning: Patient reports diarrhea for the past three days and going to the toilet around 5–6 times a day with watery, loose stools: “I've been having diarrhea for like… past three days” and “around five to six times a day… it's definitely watery. Loose stools.”
Same as cc-001: “I've been having diarrhea for like… past three days” and “around five to six times a day… it's definitely watery. Loose stools.”

Patient states the illness began with vomiting that has resolved: “it started like three days ago, and so it started with vomiting, so I vomited a couple of times, but then that went away. And, yeah, it's just diarrhea now.”

Patient feels dehydrated, weak, and has poor intake/appetite: “I feel very dehydrated… I feel like I don't drink enough… Not much [eaten]… I don't really feel like I have appetite… I feel very weak, though.”
Denies abdominal (‘tummy’) pain: Doctor asks, “any other symptoms, like tummy pain?” Patient: “Not. Not really, no.”
Denies blood in stool: Doctor asks, “Any blood in your stools?” Patient: “No, not that I could see.”
Denies headache: Doctor asks, “Any headaches or muscle pains?” Patient: “Not really.” This covers headache as not present.
Denies muscle pains (myalgia): Doctor asks, “Any headaches or muscle pains?” Patient: “Not really.” This includes absence of myalgia.
No sick contacts: Doctor asks, “Have you been around anyone unwell with diarrhea recently?” Patient: “Not that I know.”
No questionable food intake identified: Doctor asks about “takeaway food or any dodgy restaurant food?” Patient: “Not that I remember.”
Off work 3 days due to illness: Patient says, “These last three days I've been feeling really unwell, so I couldn't work.”
Asthma history: Patient states, “So I do suffer of asthma, so I do have my [in]halers…”
Uses blue inhaler as needed/infrequently: “I do have my [in]halers that I… use infrequently, let's say only when I have [symptoms].” Doctor clarifies: “Is that a blue inhaler?” Patient: “Yes, it is.”
Only current medication mentioned is the blue inhaler: After confirming inhaler use, doctor asks, “Any other medications that you take?” Patient: “No, nothing.”
There is no explicit advice to continue the asthma inhaler; inhaler use is only discussed as background: no statement like “continue using your inhaler as needed” appears in the transcript.
No known drug allergies: Doctor asks, “Do you have any allergies to any medications?” Patient: “Not that I know of.”
Father had hypertension: “My father has high… well, used to have high blood pressure.”
Father had bowel cancer and is deceased: “He actually… died of bowel cancer like 10 years ago.”
Mother has type 2 diabetes: “she has diabetes.” Doctor: “Do we know if that's type one or type two?” Patient: “It's type two.”
Lives alone: Doctor asks, “Who lives at home with you?” Patient: “Oh, I live alone.”
Occupation: “I'm a software engineer.”
Non-smoker: “I drink infrequently, like socially, let's say, and I don't smoke.”
Infrequent alcohol use: “I drink infrequently, like socially, let's say…”
No physical exam or measured temperature is documented. Patient says they feel fine now, but “currently afebrile” as a clinical finding is not explicitly stated.
Felt warm/feverish at onset: “Probably at the beginning I was feeling… I had a bit of temperature, but now I feel… kind of fine.”

Doctor diagnoses gastroenteritis and advises fluids, but does not explicitly state “self-limited,” “likely viral,” or diagnose dehydration: “I think you're probably suffering from what we call gastroenteritis… tummy bug… normally lasts for about three to five days.” Dehydration and viral etiology are inferred, not stated.
Asthma is mentioned as history with infrequent inhaler use, but there is no explicit assessment wording such as “asthma is stable.”

Doctor advises increased fluids and specific oral rehydration solution: “you can drink plenty of fluids” and “You can get things from the pharmacy, which [are] called Diurelite, which can help replenish any minerals and vitamins you may have lost… It's a type of fluid replacement drink.”
Paracetamol recommended PRN for fever/weakness: “You can take some paracetamol if you're feeling feverish and weak.”

Advised to rest/off work until diarrhea resolved 24–48 hours: “Would probably advise you to continue taking time off work for next day or two until you get better. Normally you have to be diarrhea free for about 24 to 48 hours before you return back to work.”

Doctor says, “if you're still not better next week, I want you to come back and see me,” but does not mention returning specifically for deterioration. The addition of “or if deterioration occurs” is not stated.
The plan does not address asthma management or continuing the inhaler; no such instruction appears in the transcript.
